text: Helen Hartness Flanders (May 19, 1890 – May 23, 1972), a native of Springfield, Vermont, was an internationally recognized ballad collector and authority on folk music in New England and the British Isles. At the initiative of the Vermont Commission on Country Life, she began a three-decade career collecting traditional songs from New England, many of which originated in the British Isles, during a time when people were shifting away from traditional music in favor of radio. Recognizing that these songs were at risk of being lost as the people who sang them passed away, Flanders dedicated herself to recording them. She was born in Springfield, where her father, James Hartness, was an inventor, industrialist, and one-term Governor of Vermont, and she graduated from the Dana Hall School in 1909, singing in the glee club and joining the French club. In 1911, she married Ralph Flanders, a mechanical engineer, industrialist, and U.S. Senator from Vermont (1946–1959), with whom she maintained homes in Springfield and Washington, D.C., entertaining notable figures such as Dorothy Canfield Fisher and Robert Frost. They had three children: Elizabeth (born 1912), Anna (also known as Nancy, born 1918), and James (born 1923); Elizabeth assisted her mother in collecting and transcribing songs. Flanders published two volumes of poetry and one children's play, and traveled with her husband to the British Isles, Europe, and Australia. In 1930, Vermont Governor John E. Weeks invited her to join the Committee on Traditions and Ideals of the Vermont Commission on Country Life, which tasked her with collecting Vermont folk songs passed down orally. Initially recording on wax cylinders, she later used aluminum and acetate discs from 1939 to 1949 and reel-to-reel tapes, often using her car’s cigarette lighter when electricity was unavailable. She worked with George Brown in 1930, Phillips Barry from 1931 to 1937, and Alan Lomax in 1939; from 1940 to 1958, Marguerite Olney made major contributions to both collection management and fieldwork. Between 1930 and 1939, she focused on Child ballads, resulting in a large number of cylinder recordings; of the 150 disc recordings with Lomax, many included songs, stories, and fiddle tunes. Over time, her recordings expanded to include religious songs, children's songs, 19th-century American popular songs, dance tunes, and folktales. George Brown, Alice Brown, Phillips Barry, Marguerite Olney, and Elizabeth Flanders Ballard all created musical transcriptions for her publications. An index of all recordings (collected between 1930 and 1958) was published in 1983. In 1941, due to insufficient space in her home, she donated the collection to Middlebury College, Vermont, where it is now housed in Special Collections and includes nearly 4,500 field recordings, her papers, and related materials. Copies are also available at the American Folklife Center of the Library of Congress and Harvard University, which holds files of her correspondence. Flanders observed that songs migrating from the British Isles or Europe often changed as singers incorporated details from life in the New World, such as the "Yorkshire Bite" becoming the "New Hampshire Bite," and many ballads reflect aspects of New England and Colonial history. In 1942, Middlebury College awarded her an honorary Master of Arts; she was a member of the National Committee of the National Folk Festival Association and vice president of the Folksong Society of the Northeast, and in 1966, the Vermont House of Representatives added her name to the state’s Roll of Distinction in the Arts. She authored eight books on ballads and folk music, wrote pamphlets, newspaper and magazine articles, and two books of poetry, and contributed a regular column on ballads to the Springfield Sunday Union and Republican (Massachusetts) during the 1930s. Folksingers such as Margaret MacArthur (1928–2006), who moved to Vermont in the late 1940s, promoted the collection through concerts and recordings, with Flanders encouraging her and providing copies of the recordings; MacArthur became known for her repertoire of songs from the Flanders Collection.
